transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Yeah, thank you. Um, well, it’s... it’s kind of a lot of things building up over time, I guess. I'm a software developer, and I've been doing this for a long time, but lately... well, what finally pushed me to come in today—and honestly, it took me about three weeks just to actually make the appointment because I kept getting sidetracked every time I picked up my phone—is that I just can’t seem to organize the moving parts anymore. 

My work, my life, it's all just... it's like a giant knot I can't untangle. I have all these different plates spinning at once. I’ve got these patent notes for a new software architecture we're building, which is huge and needs my full attention, and then there’s all this workshop prep I need to do, plus these gallery deadlines for a digital art project I'm involved in, and on top of that, the constant, everyday team decisions I have to manage for my junior devs at the office. It's just so much data coming at me all the time. 

And instead of looking at it logically—like, you know, prioritizing what needs to happen first, second, and third like a normal person with a graduate degree should be able to do—I sit down at my desk and I just get pulled in five different directions. I end up starting whatever is loudest instead of what actually matters. Like, if someone pings me on our work chat about a tiny, insignificant bug, I'll completely drop the patent notes and spend three hours on the bug, just because the notification made a sound and it was right there in front of my face. And then the whole day is gone, and the really important stuff is still sitting there, untouched. It's incredibly frustrating, and I'm just exhausted from constantly putting out the nearest fire instead of actually building anything.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge when faced with these multiple tasks and responsibilities?

Anxious? Um... I don't know if I'd call it anxious, exactly. Like, I don't get that physical panic, you know? My heart isn't racing, I'm not sweating, I'm not sitting there dreading that something terrible is going to happen. It's not like that. It's more just... a total system overload. 

Like, take last Tuesday. I sat down at my desk at 8:30 AM, coffee in hand, completely intending to draft the first section of those patent notes. I had my dual monitors set up, my noise-canceling headphones on, ready to go. But then I saw my inbox had 47 unread emails, and my brain just sort of... stopped. It wasn't fear, it was just this blank wall. I couldn't decide if I should read the emails first so they wouldn't distract me, or ignore them and start the notes, or maybe just check the Slack channel to make sure the junior devs weren't stuck on something. 

And instead of feeling "on edge," I just felt this bizarre, heavy paralysis. I ended up just staring at the screen for maybe twenty minutes, opening and closing tabs, completely unable to pick a starting point. It's like having a computer with too many heavy applications running at the same time—the fan is spinning like crazy, but the screen is just frozen on the loading wheel. So, yeah, I don't think it's anxiety. It's just... I just don't know how to process it all when there's that much volume. It's more frustrating than anything else, really, just sitting there knowing I have a master's degree and I can't even figure out which window to click on first.
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you, even when you're trying to focus on a task?

Oh, constantly. It's... it's honestly ridiculous. You know, working in tech, especially when you're overseeing other developers, you're sort of expected to be plugged into the matrix all the time. We use Slack for all our internal communications, and I've actually tried to optimize it. I went into the settings and made it so it only notifies me for direct mentions or critical channel updates, because I know how bad I get with this. 

But even with all those safeguards, if Slack pings—just that tiny little sound—or if I have a browser tab open for some API documentation and it flashes because a background script refreshed, it's like a physical pull. I just have to look. And it's not even just the external stuff on the screen, either. Half the time, I'll be right in the middle of writing a really complex block of code, where I'm holding all the logic and variables in my head, and suddenly a visual idea for that digital art project I mentioned earlier just pops into my brain. Like, completely out of nowhere, I'll think about a new shader effect or a specific color gradient for the gallery piece.

And the absolute second that happens, I completely lose the thread of what I was coding. The whole mental model just evaporates. And instead of just jotting the idea down on a sticky note and getting back to work like I should, I'll open up a new tab to look up a reference image for that gradient. And then I'm reading an article about color theory, and then I'm looking at SVG animation libraries on GitHub, and suddenly twenty minutes have gone by—sometimes way more—and I've spent all this time following some totally unrelated design rabbit hole. 

And the worst part is, after I finally snap out of it, I have to look back at my code editor and try to figure out what line I was on and what the function was even supposed to do. It takes me another fifteen minutes just to rebuild the context I lost. It's like I have zero filter for incoming stimuli. If it catches my attention, whether it's a notification on my monitor or just a random thought in my own head, I just veer right off the road to go chase it. I've tried putting my phone in another room, but when your entire job is on a computer, you can't exactly hide the internet from yourself, you know? It's just always right there, and I just can't seem to block any of it out.
Have you always had difficulty focusing and managing multiple tasks, or is this a relatively new challenge for you?

Well, you know, I used to think it was just the tech industry, right? Like, the burnout, the constant screen time, getting my master's degree and taking on more responsibility as I got older. I kept telling myself, "Oh, you're 46, you're managing a team now, of course you're overwhelmed, anyone would be." But... honestly? No. No, it's not new at all. 

If I really sit down and look back, way back, this exact same pattern was there when I was just a little kid in grade school. Long before I was even a teenager, long before I had a smartphone or a Slack account or a dual-monitor setup to blame it on. I actually found some of my old report cards when I was helping my parents clear out their attic a few years ago. My mom kept everything in these big plastic bins, you know the ones? Anyway, I was looking through them, and the comments from my teachers were... well, it was almost eerie reading them now, considering what I'm dealing with at work. 

Every single year, it was the exact same script. They would always write that I was a bright kid, that I had a lot of potential and grasped the concepts quickly, but then the very next sentence was always about how I spent half the day daydreaming. Just totally checked out, staring at the wall. And the assignments! Oh man. It wasn't even that I didn't do the work. I would actually sit at the kitchen table, do the entire math worksheet, put it in my backpack... and then the next day, the teacher would ask for it, and I just couldn't produce it. I was constantly losing my homework folders. Just, totally gone. Or I'd find the finished assignment three weeks later, completely crumpled up at the bottom of my desk or shoved inside a textbook I hadn't opened. 

It used to drive my parents absolutely crazy because they knew I knew the material, but my grades never reflected it because I just couldn't manage the physical pieces of paper. So, yeah, this whole inability to organize moving parts and stay focused on what's in front of me? It’s been happening my entire life. It just looks different now because instead of losing a blue paper folder, I'm losing my train of thought on a massive software architecture project. But the underlying... whatever it is, that disconnect? It's exactly the same as when I was eight years old. I just didn't realize it until everything got so complex as an adult that my old coping mechanisms just completely collapsed under the weight of it all.
Do you often act on impulse without fully thinking through the consequences?

Act on impulse? No... no, I really wouldn't say so. In fact, it's almost the exact opposite for me. I am definitely not the guy who just jumps out of an airplane without checking the parachute, you know? If anything, I overthink everything to the point of absolute exhaustion. I get completely bogged down in the details before I make any kind of move.

Like, just to give you an example, my wife and I were looking to buy a new espresso machine a couple of months ago. Our old one, this basic little model we'd had for like six years, finally gave out. The pump just died on a Tuesday morning. Now, most people would probably just go to the store, look at a few boxes, maybe read a review or two on Amazon, and just buy a replacement, right? Not me. I literally spent three weeks researching boiler types. I had a whole spreadsheet going on my second monitor, comparing dual boilers versus heat exchangers, PID temperature controls, rotary versus vibratory pumps. I was watching hour-long YouTube teardowns of high-end Italian espresso machines at two in the morning. I couldn't just *buy* one. I had to know every possible consequence of the purchase, how easy it was to source replacement gaskets, what the water pressure consistency was like... it was ridiculous. 

And it's exactly like that at work, too. I don't just push code to production on a whim or make snap decisions. I'm terrified of breaking the build or messing up the architecture. I'll sit there and review my own pull request three or four times, checking every single variable and edge case, because I'm so worried about missing something that might cause a cascade failure down the line. 

So, no, jumping the gun or acting without thinking? That's really not me at all. I get stuck in the thinking part. I mean, sure, I might get distracted by a random thought, like I was saying about the digital art stuff earlier, but that's just my attention drifting away. That's not me making a rash, impulsive decision that actually affects my life or my job or my finances. When it comes to actual actions, I'm practically paralyzed by trying to think through *all* the consequences. It actually drives my wife crazy sometimes. She'll just want to go out for dinner, and she's like, "Just pick a restaurant!" and I'm sitting there reading Yelp reviews from three years ago trying to figure out if the parking situation is going to be a nightmare or if the menu has changed. So, yeah, impulsivity isn't really my problem. If anything, I could probably stand to be a little *more* impulsive, just to save myself the headache of analyzing every little thing to death.
Do you experience significant emotional distress as a result of your difficulties with organization and focus?

Oh God, yes. It's... it's honestly keeping me up at night. The stress of it is just eating me alive lately, because it’s not just a private struggle anymore, you know? For a long time, I could kind of mask it, or work a twelve-hour day to make up for the six hours I spent distracted. But now... it’s actually starting to really damage my work reputation. And when you're 46, and you've spent your entire adult life—ever since grad school—building up this image of being a reliable, senior-level developer, watching that crumble is just... it's devastating. 

Like, to give you an idea of how bad it's getting, just a few weeks ago I completely missed a critical patent filing checkpoint. This was for a proprietary data pipeline I’d actually conceptualized, something I was really proud of. But there were all these moving parts with the legal team, specific forms, specific formatting for the technical diagrams, and a hard deadline. And I had the emails, I had the calendar alerts, but I got so derailed trying to perfect one tiny, insignificant piece of the documentation that I completely lost track of the actual submission process. I missed the window. The legal team was furious, my director had to get involved to do damage control, and I just felt physically sick to my stomach. I mean, I was sitting at my desk just shaking, wondering how I let that happen.

And then, right on the heels of that disaster, we had this massive, highly anticipated architecture review. I was supposed to be the one driving it. But because my focus has been so fragmented, I hadn't organized the dependencies properly, and my presentation was just a mess. I was jumping from one concept to another, losing my place... it was an incredibly difficult review. The principal engineers were asking me totally reasonable questions about our scaling strategy, and I was just blanking, fumbling through my notes, completely unable to pull the cohesive picture together. 

It was humiliating. I could literally see my collaborators exchanging these looks across the conference table. And the worst part is, ever since that meeting, there's been this very obvious, uncomfortable undercurrent where they are actively questioning whether I can actually lead the larger project moving forward. I've been CC'd on emails where they're subtly suggesting we bring in a co-lead, which is just corporate speak for "we don't trust you to handle this." So, yes, the emotional distress is... it's overwhelming. It breaks my heart, because I know the technology inside and out, but my brain just won't let me organize it to prove that to anyone anymore. I just feel like my entire career is slipping through my fingers and I can't seem to stop it.
Are your difficulties with organization and focus affecting your personal relationships, such as with your wife or friends?

Affecting my personal relationships? You know... surprisingly, no. Not really. I mean, you'd think so, right? With how much of a disaster my work life is right now, you'd assume my home life is falling apart too, but... no, it’s actually okay. 

My wife and I, we've been together a long time, and she just... she knows how I am. I mean, sure, she gets a little exasperated sometimes, like with the whole espresso machine research thing I mentioned, or if I totally zone out while she’s telling me about her day. Sometimes she literally has to wave her hand in front of my face and go, "Hello? Earth to husband?" But it never turns into a real fight. It’s more of a running joke between us. And honestly, a big part of why it doesn't cause major issues in our marriage is because she is just incredibly organized herself. She naturally took over all the household logistics years ago. She handles the bills, she keeps the shared Google Calendar for appointments, she knows exactly when the cars need their oil changed or when the dog needs his shots. 

If it were up to me to remember all those moving parts, yeah, we'd probably be living in absolute chaos and she’d be furious with me all the time. But because she manages the administrative side of our lives, my inability to organize things doesn't really blow up in my face at home. The stakes are just so much lower. If I forget to move the laundry to the dryer, or if I start cleaning the garage and get distracted by an old box of cables and leave everything in a mess... it’s just a minor annoyance to her, not a catastrophic failure like missing a legal patent deadline, you know? 

And as for friends... I’m 46, so it’s not like I have this massive, demanding social life to keep track of anyway. I have a few close buddies from grad school, and our friendships are just very... low-maintenance. We might grab a beer once a month, or we just hop on Discord on a Friday night to play some games. There’s no real pressure to perform or organize anything. If I forget to text someone back for three days because I read the message, thought of a reply, and then completely lost my train of thought before I hit send... they don't take it personally. They’re all busy guys in the industry too, so they get it. We just pick up right where we left off. 

So, yeah, the social and personal side of things is actually fine. It’s really just the professional sphere where everything is completely collapsing on me, because the complexity is so high and I don't have my wife there to manage the calendar and cover for my blind spots.
Are you having trouble completing everyday tasks at home due to your difficulties with focus and organization?

Everyday tasks? No, honestly, I don't have any real trouble getting those done. It’s funny, because you'd think my brain would be just as scattered at home as it is at the office, but it’s really not. I think it’s because the stakes are so much lower, and the tasks are just... tangible. You know? Like, if I need to clean the kitchen, I can see the dirty dishes, I can see the counter getting wiped down. There’s a clear beginning, middle, and end, unlike a massive software architecture project where the end goal is always shifting and abstract. 

Like, take my weekend routine, for example. Every Saturday morning, I have this whole ritual. I wake up around 7:00, I go downstairs, and I make coffee—using that new espresso machine I was telling you about earlier, the one I spent three weeks researching. I ended up going with the dual boiler, by the way, and it was absolutely the right call, the temperature stability is just incredible. Anyway, I make my cappuccino, and then I take our dog, Buster—he's a Golden Retriever mix, about six years old—I take him for a solid 45-minute walk around the neighborhood. Then I come back, I mow the lawn, I trim the hedges, I might fix a leaky faucet if we have one... I just sort of knock things out. 

My wife usually leaves a little handwritten list on the fridge for me, just basic bullet points, and I actually find it really satisfying to just cross them off one by one with a Sharpie. I don't get paralyzed or stuck the way I do with my code. I just do it. Even cooking... I usually cook dinner three nights a week, and I never leave it half-finished. I'll spend two hours making a from-scratch bolognese sauce, simmering it, getting the seasoning just right, and I stay totally locked in on it. It actually feels good to just chop onions and garlic and not have to think about data pipelines. 

So, no, the day-to-day stuff, the basic living tasks... I really don't struggle with completing those at all. It's almost like a relief to just do normal, physical chores. As long as it's something straightforward around the house, I can finish it without any real issue.
Do you often feel restless or fidgety when you're sitting still?

Restless? Yeah... yeah, actually I do. It's funny you ask that because it's something I've been noticing a lot more lately, especially since my setup at home is where I take all my meetings now. You know, when you're in a physical conference room at the corporate office, there's a certain decorum, you kind of just force yourself to sit still because everyone is right there next to you. But in my home office... man, it's a whole different story. 

We have these incredibly long design calls for the new platform. I'm talking two, sometimes two and a half hours of just staring at a grid of faces on a screen, debating microservices architecture or whatever. And when I'm just sitting there, after about twenty minutes, I start to get this... this really intense physical sensation. It's like this literal pressure building up inside my body, right in my chest and down into my legs, just screaming at me that I need to move. I physically cannot just sit in my desk chair for that long without feeling like I'm going to jump out of my skin. 

So I end up getting up and just pacing around my office. I'll walk back and forth behind my desk, or I'll move over to the little armchair I have in the corner for reading, and then a few minutes later I'll shift back to the main desk chair. I'm just constantly shifting from chair to chair, or standing up and pacing. And the whole time, I'm trying so hard to keep my eyes on the monitor and nod at the right times, trying to look like I'm completely locked in and focused on the presentation. Because, you know, the webcam is on, and especially with everyone doubting me lately, I really don't want the principal engineers thinking I'm blowing off the meeting or not paying attention. But it takes so much energy just to manage that physical need to move while trying to maintain this facade of being the calm, collected senior developer. I even looked into buying one of those under-desk treadmills last week just to give my legs something to do, because the pressure to just get up and move is so overwhelming when I'm supposed to be perfectly still.
Are you feeling like your difficulties with organization and focus are affecting your overall sense of well-being?

Affecting my well-being? Yeah. Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it's honestly destroying my peace of mind right now. You know, I’ve always prided myself on being the guy people come to for solutions. I'm a senior developer, I've been in this industry for over two decades, and my entire sense of self is really tied up in being competent and reliable. But lately... it’s just, it’s starting to actively damage my reputation at work, and that is taking a massive toll on me mentally. 

Like, for example, just a couple of weeks ago, we had this crucial patent filing checkpoint. It was for a new data ingestion algorithm I actually helped conceptualize, so it was a big deal. The legal team had sent over a checklist of documentation they needed by a specific Tuesday. And I... I honestly don't even know what happened. I saw the email, I know I flagged it, I even made a mental note to pull the technical specs from the repository, but then I got pulled into some random bug fix, and the entire patent deadline just completely evaporated from my brain. I completely missed the checkpoint. The legal guys were incredibly frustrated, my manager had to step in to smooth things over... it was just humiliating. 

And the thing is, it's not even just the administrative, paperwork side of things anymore. It's bleeding into the actual core engineering work, which is what really terrifies me. We had this major architecture review a few days after that whole patent disaster. It was supposed to be my project, right? I'm the one who is supposed to be leading this massive transition to a new platform. But during the review, I was just so scattered. My notes were a complete mess, I couldn't locate the sequence diagrams I had made, and when the other engineers started probing into the edge cases, I just... I totally blanked. I was rambling, I couldn't hold the thread of the conversation, and it turned into this incredibly difficult, painful meeting. 

And the worst part is, I could see it on their faces on the screen. You know that look? That sort of polite, uncomfortable silence where everyone is just staring at you? After the call, my manager pulled me into a quick one-on-one, and he actually asked—he literally said it out loud—if I was sure I had the bandwidth to lead this larger project. My own collaborators are actively questioning whether I can actually do this. They're doubting my ability to lead. So, yeah, when you ask about my overall well-being... I'm barely sleeping. I'm just constantly terrified that everyone is finally realizing I'm dropping the ball, and I have this constant, heavy knot in my stomach every single time I log on for the day. It's exhausting.
Are there any areas of your life outside of work where you feel like your difficulties with organization and focus are causing problems?

Outside of work? No... no, I really haven't noticed it causing any issues there. I mean, like I was saying earlier about the chores and the cooking, my personal life is actually pretty well-ordered. It's almost like a completely different brain is operating when I log off for the day. 

Take my hobbies, for instance. I'm really into woodworking—just amateur stuff, mostly out in the garage. I spent about three months last winter building this custom mid-century modern credenza for our dining room. Walnut veneer, solid brass hardware, the whole nine yards. And when I'm out there measuring cuts, setting up the router table, sanding things down... I am completely dialed in. I don't lose my pencil, I don't forget my measurements, I don't get distracted and leave a joint half-glued. I can spend four hours on a Saturday just meticulously sanding and applying Danish oil, coat after coat, and I never lose focus. 

Same with my friendships, or my marriage. My wife handles some of the bigger calendar stuff, sure, but I never forget our anniversary, I never miss a dinner reservation. Even the boring administrative life stuff, like getting the cars inspected or paying the property taxes, I just have a system for it and it works. I've got everything on autopay, or I just deal with it the minute the mail comes in. I take the car to the shop down the street—the one on Elm, they've known me for ten years, great guys—and I never miss a mileage milestone for an oil change. It's just not a problem. 

So, honestly, no. It’s really just the job. It’s like the second I sit down at that desk and look at a code repository, all my ability to organize my thoughts just completely evaporates. But the rest of my life? The rest of my life is actually perfectly fine. Well, I mean, aside from the stress of work hanging over my head and ruining my mood, obviously, but the actual focus issues just don't seem to happen when I'm off the clock.
Do you often feel restless or fidgety in situations where you're not working, like when you're watching a movie or reading a book?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because I know I just went on and on about how my woodworking and all that is perfectly fine. But woodworking is active, you know? I'm on my feet, I'm using my hands, I'm moving around the garage. When it comes to something completely passive, like just sitting still... yeah, actually, it is a bit of a problem. 

I notice it the most after I've been doing late-night work. In my role, I often have to do these off-hours deployments, pushing updates to the servers at like 11 PM or midnight when user traffic is at its lowest. So I'll finally finish up, log off, shut the laptop, and I'll go downstairs to the living room. The house is completely quiet, my wife is already asleep, and I'll think to myself, 'Okay, I'm just going to sit quietly for a bit, or maybe read a chapter of a book.' I always try to pick something completely nontechnical, like historical nonfiction or a biography, just to get my brain entirely out of the software architecture space. 

But I sit down on the couch, and within a few minutes—I mean literally two or three minutes—I'm tapping my foot against the rug. Or I'm drumming my fingers on the cover of the book. I just can't seem to sink into the cushions and relax. I'll read maybe half a page, and then I'm instinctively grabbing my phone off the coffee table to check the news, or look at the weather for tomorrow, or just scroll through absolutely nothing. And if I'm not doing that, I'm getting up because I suddenly feel the urge to go adjust the thermostat, or I notice the throw blanket is folded wrong so I have to get up and fix it. I'm just constantly getting up to adjust something or finding an excuse to move around instead of actually winding down. 

It's incredibly frustrating because I am genuinely exhausted at that point. I want to rest. But it's like the momentum from the workday is still physically trapped in my muscles, and even though I just want to sit in the quiet and read my book about the Wright brothers, I'm sitting there vibrating, checking my screen, getting up, sitting back down... it completely defeats the purpose of trying to have a quiet moment. So, yeah, if I'm not actively working with my hands, sitting still is... it's a challenge.
Are there any daily activities beyond work where you feel your difficulties with focus and organization are causing significant problems?

I think I mentioned this a little bit earlier when we were talking about my hobbies and the house stuff, but really, no. I genuinely don't feel like the focus and organization issues are bleeding into my daily life outside of the office. It's almost bizarre how compartmentalized it is. 

Like, if you look at my weekend errands, or just the day-to-day household management... I'm actually the organized one in the house. Take grocery shopping, for example. I do all the grocery shopping for us, usually on Sunday mornings right after they open at 7 AM to beat the rush. And I don't just wander around the aisles hoping I remember what we need or getting distracted. I have this whole system on my phone—it's a shared list app that syncs with my wife's phone, and I actually have it categorized by the physical layout of the specific grocery store we go to. The big one over on Maple. I have it set up so it goes produce first, then the deli, then the dry goods, then dairy at the back... I walk in, I get exactly what's on the list, I don't get sidetracked by random endcap displays or forget what I came for, and I'm out of there in twenty minutes flat. I never forget the milk, I never lose my train of thought in the middle of the frozen food aisle. 

Or even just the daily stuff, you know? Like making sure the trash and recycling are out on Tuesday nights, or keeping the kitchen island clear of mail. I don't need reminders for that stuff, I just do it. It's like my brain has absolutely no problem sequencing and executing those physical, real-world tasks. I can follow a recipe, I can manage the household budget, I can plan a weekend trip down to the hour. It's really only when I'm sitting in front of that monitor, trying to juggle abstract software architecture and corporate deadlines, that my organization just completely falls apart. So, yeah, beyond the job, my daily activities are completely fine. I don't have any problems there at all. It's just the work.
Are there any other areas of your daily life beyond work and relationships where you feel like your difficulties with organization and focus are causing significant problems?

No, honestly, like I keep trying to explain, it really is just confined to my job. There's no other area of my life that's falling apart like this. But... man, when I say it's affecting my work, I don't just mean I'm personally frustrated or having a hard time getting through the day. It's actually gotten to the point where it is actively damaging my professional reputation, which is incredibly hard to swallow after being in this industry for over twenty years. 

Just to give you an idea of how bad it's getting, we have this internal innovation program at the company, right? I had this genuinely solid concept for a new data caching mechanism, something that could really optimize our server loads. I did the initial technical write-up, leadership was excited about it, but then there's this whole bureaucratic process to actually get the patent filed. You have to coordinate with the internal legal team, fill out specific documentation, do prior art searches, hit these very strict quarterly deadlines... and I just completely dropped the ball. I had all the technical specs, but every time I tried to sit down and organize the actual submission paperwork, my brain just felt like it was walking through wet cement. I kept putting it off, losing track of the email threads, and I ended up completely missing a major, hard checkpoint for the filing. The legal department had already allocated budget for external counsel to review it, and my manager actually had to step in and formally apologize on my behalf. It was humiliating. 

And then, if that wasn't bad enough, we had this massive architecture review a few weeks ago. I'm a senior developer, so I'm supposed to be the one leading this transition to a new microservices setup we're doing. But during the review meeting with all the stakeholders, I was just... a mess. I hadn't organized my slides right, I couldn't find the specific sequence diagrams when the infrastructure guys asked for them, and when they started firing off complex, multi-part questions, I just kept losing my train of thought entirely. I was rambling, I was disorganized, I looked completely unprepared even though I know the system inside and out. It was a really difficult meeting, and the fallout from it has been awful. I actually found out from a colleague that some of the main collaborators on the project went to my director afterward and started questioning whether I can even handle leading the larger project. They literally asked if someone else needed to step in and take over the technical lead because I seemed so scattered and unreliable. 

So, I know you're asking about outside of work, but I just... I can't stress enough that while my home life is completely fine, my career is practically hanging by a thread because of this. People are starting to think I'm incompetent, and I don't know how to fix it.
Do you think your main problem is that you can't focus and pay attention, or that you're too restless and can't sit still?

Man, that is... I really don't know if I can give you a straight answer on that. I'm honestly not sure which one I'd call the main problem, because they both just feel so overwhelming in their own specific contexts, you know? 

Like, if you're looking at the actual fallout in my life right now, obviously the focus and attention stuff at work is the most destructive. I mean, I just spent all that time telling you about the patent filing I messed up and that disaster of an architecture review, and how my colleagues are literally questioning my competence because I can't keep my thoughts organized or pay attention during complex technical discussions. That's the stuff that genuinely terrifies me, because it's twenty years of a professional reputation on the line. It's actively damaging my livelihood. 

But then... then I think about the restlessness. And even though getting up to adjust the thermostat or tapping my foot while I try to read a historical biography isn't going to get me fired, it's just so deeply, deeply exhausting on a personal level. It's like I was saying earlier, I'll be sitting in the living room at midnight, the house is dead quiet, I'm physically tired from the day, and my body just refuses to power down. The focus issues feel like my brain is walking through wet cement when I need it to sprint, but the restlessness feels like my engine is just constantly revving at a red light when all I want to do is turn the car off and rest. 

So... I really don't know. I couldn't tell you which one is the primary issue or the root cause.
